You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

The test failure is related to PolynomialFitter.fit(double[] guess) method, which internally calls fit with a parametric polynomial function and the initial guess. The current bug report states that new multivariate optimizers create a full nxn matrix when using a weights vector of size n, causing memory exhaustion for large n (e.g. 4120 points). In the testLargeSample, the fitter adds 40,000 observed points, a very large number, which likely produces this memory overuse.

The PolynomialFitter internally uses multivariate vector optimizers (e.g. LevenbergMarquardtOptimizer) which are mentioned in the bug report. When large data sets are passed as observed points, the optimizer attempts to build a full Jacobian/Hessian matrix of size roughly n x n, with n the number of weights (parameters). This matrix creation and copying exhaust memory resources during fitting large samples, which is the testLargeSample scenario.

Since the test tries to fit polynomials of degree 0 to 9 with 40,000 points each, the dimension of the parameter vector is degree+1 (from 1 to 10), but the number of points is very large at 40,000. The bug report however describes memory exhaustion occurring when the "weights" vector size is large (e.g. >4000). Possibly, internally a large weight vector is created which leads to a full nxn matrix. The bug report points to an inefficiency in the treatment of weights passed to the multivariate vector optimizers.

From this reasoning, the root cause is the internal usage of full dense matrices of size quadratic in the number of weights in the multivariate vector optimizer used by PolynomialFitter. When a weight vector (for each data point) is used, it's internally treated as a full matrix, causing memory exhaustion. This leads to failure or performance issues in testLargeSample when large data sets are used.

No other recent issue reports are closely related to this memory issue with vector weights and large number of points.

In summary, the failing test exposes a memory inefficiency in the optimizer's handling of weights or points, causing full quadratic memory usage and resulting in exhaustion. This is the core reason the test fails: the optimizer and PolynomialFitter design do not scale well to large numbers of data points or weight vectors.

# Diagnosis

The failing test `testLargeSample` in `PolynomialFitterTest` adds a very large number (40,000) of observed points to the `PolynomialFitter`, which then fits a polynomial model using the `LevenbergMarquardtOptimizer` (a multivariate vector optimizer). The current bug report indicates that passing a large weight vector to such optimizers creates an nxn full matrix copy, resulting in excessive memory use and eventual failure.

The `PolynomialFitter.fit(double[] guess)` method triggers fitting via such an optimizer internally, passing all observed points. When the number of data points or weights is large, this causes the optimizer to allocate a large dense matrix with size quadratic in the number of weights/parameters, which exhausts memory. Thus, the test fails because the optimizer struggles to handle large data with the current internal implementation of weight handling and matrix creation.

This memory inefficiency in handling weights and large input data in the multivariate vector optimizer directly causes the test failure with large samples. The issue arises in the interaction between `PolynomialFitter`, its underlying optimizer, and their treatment of weight vectors as full nxn matrices, leading to excessive memory consumption and failure on large inputs.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
